conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for coming in today. My name is Dr. Rivera and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician; I spend my days supporting new mothers as they navigate all the emotional ups-and-downs that can arrive after a baby is born.  

Right now I’d like to do a quick check-in with a standard questionnaire called the EPDS. It’s simply a set of ten questions that asks how you’ve been feeling over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share is confidential. My only goal is to make sure you feel heard, supported, and safe.  

We can take the questions at whatever pace feels comfortable for you; each one is short, and we’ll be finished in just a few minutes. Whenever you’re ready, we can start with the first question.

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—would you say you’ve enjoyed laughing as much as you usually do?

[soft half-smile that fades quickly]

I… I can still laugh, I guess, but it feels kind of forced. Like, if my husband makes a joke I’ll smile, but it doesn’t feel the same—doesn’t bubble up the way it used to. Most of the time I’m just too worn out to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, yes, technically I laugh sometimes, but it’s pretty rare and it doesn’t feel natural. Mostly I’m just too tired or worried to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much lately. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk outside—but now it all feels like one more thing I have to get through. I still try, because I know I “should,” but the enjoyment part just isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle or if I can’t get her to nap, I keep thinking it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m already failing her. Even little stuff, like forgetting to pack enough diapers in the bag, spirals into “I’m a terrible mom.” I know in my head it’s not all on me, but the guilt just pops up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly imagine her choking, or I’ll lie down and picture something awful happening in her crib. There’s no real reason—she’s healthy, the doctor says everything’s fine—but my mind keeps spinning through these scary “what-ifs.” I can usually talk myself down after a while, but it’s exhausting when it happens over and over.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a tightness in my chest that comes out of nowhere—like I’m bracing for something awful to happen, even when everything’s quiet. I’ll be rocking the baby in the dark and suddenly feel my heart racing, convinced I’m missing something dangerous. It passes after a few minutes, but in the moment it feels like I can’t catch my breath.
Things have been getting on top of me

A lot of the time. Between the night feedings, the piles of laundry, and just trying to keep her content, it feels like I’m barely treading water. I manage the basics—she’s fed, changed, loved—but everything else, including taking care of myself, seems impossible. I keep thinking, “How can such a tiny baby need so much, and why can’t I handle it better?”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I lie down exhausted, but my head just keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” and everything I think I messed up that day. Even when she’s sleeping, I’ll wake up every hour checking the monitor, heart pounding, sure I heard her cry. By the time I drift off it’s almost time for the next feed, so I’m running on these short broken bits of sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days, yeah. It’s like a gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll look at her little face and feel this rush of love, but then the sadness creeps back in—this heavy, empty feeling I can’t shake. Some afternoons I just sit on the couch with her asleep on my chest and cry, even though I can’t always name why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it hits me three, maybe four times a week. Sometimes it’s because I’m overtired or she won’t stop fussing, but other times it just leaks out—like yesterday when I folded her tiny onesies and suddenly felt like I was drowning. The tears come fast, and once they start it’s hard to turn them off.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… never. I feel awful a lot of the time, but I would never want to leave her or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You have shared that the past few weeks since your baby arrived have felt overwhelmingly heavy-laughter rarely feels natural, enjoyable moments are scarce, and a constant stream of worries and self-criticism keeps you on edge. You described feeling like you are "treading water," waking through the night to check the monitor, and crying several times a week even when you cannot name a clear reason. Despite these painful feelings, you remain devoted to your daughter and want desperately to feel better so you can be the mother you believe she deserves.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is rare and unnatural, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports significant loss of anticipatory pleasure, clearly "definitely less than" before, matching option score 2.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense self-blame for routine infant-care challenges, matching 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily intrusive worries and "what-ifs" happening "over and over," matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic episodes (tight chest, racing heart, breathlessness) that occur "sometimes"—direct semantic match to "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nearly constant sleep disruption due to persistent anxious thoughts and hypervigilance, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness that occurs "most days" and feels like an unshakable "gray cloud," matching the "most of the time" severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying episodes 3-4 times weekly with emotional triggers, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating a high likelihood of major depressive episode with peripartum onset. You endorsed high scores on nine of ten items, meeting core criteria: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, fatigue and worthlessness, concentration difficulties, sleep disturbance, psychomotor agitation, and recurrent anxiety. These findings align closely with clinical features outlined in the <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within the next week
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, and compatible antidepressant options
3. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
4. Share these results with your partner or trusted family member and enlist practical help overnight when possible
5. Connect with local <med>postpartum support group</med> or <med>PMAD peer support program</med> for validation and coping strategies
6. Practice short self-care routines: five-minute outdoor walk, balanced snacks, and brief breathing exercises during naps
7. Plan a safety check-in-call 988 or local emergency services if you ever notice thoughts of self-harm, even passively
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Post-partum depression/anxiety screening – 10-item EPDS responses reviewed  
Patient is 3–4 wks post-delivery, exclusively caring for infant.

Key endorsed symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” crying 3–4×/week (Q8–9)  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal enjoyment, activities feel obligatory (Q1–2)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re parenting competence (Q3)  
- Intrusion of “what-if” fears, nocturnal hyper-vigilance, panic-like episodes with chest tightness & breathlessness (Q4–5)  
- Sleep disruption driven by rumination and safety checking (Q7)  
- Frequent sense of being overwhelmed, “treading water,” neglecting self-care (Q6)

Pattern: symptoms present “most days,” cause functional impairment, no discrete manic/hypomanic features.  
No self-harm ideation reported (Q10); no current safety concern.

Screening significance  
Score profile suggests moderate–high probability of major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety in postpartum context; meets threshold for further evaluation (diagnostic interview, risk assessment, review of medical contributors, consideration of supports/resources).
